events.text: Objective: Determine whether Hellberg Safety should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources for evidence; financial data may not be available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify a specific use case and target consumer segment.; Must consider existing B2B/industrial focus and potential brand perception.; Must evaluate alternatives including no expansion, product redesign, new distribution route, or new customer group.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., recreational shooting, outdoor sports, or home DIY) with dedicated branding and direct-to-consumer sales.; 2) Expand the existing hearing-protection line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., musicians, sleep aid) without a separate brand, using current distribution channels.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B/industrial hearing and face protection offerings.; 4) Redesign existing products for consumer appeal (e.g., fashion, comfort) while keeping the same brand and distribution.; 5) Partner with or license the brand to third-party consumer retailers to reach individual buyers without direct investment..

T1: Consumers will adopt hearing protection for recreational activities (e.g., shooting, hunting, outdoor sports) if they perceive it as enhancing performance and safety without compromising enjoyment. Who benefits: Recreational users who need situational awareness and comfort while engaging in noisy activities.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it mutes sound and reduces enjoyment; a product that preserves audio clarity and comfort would remove that barrier.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for specialized features (e.g., active listening, FM radio) and sell directly to consumers through e-commerce, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Recreational market size is sufficient to justify dedicated product line.; Consumers are willing to pay for performance-enhancing features.; Brand perception of safety does not deter recreational buyers.. Predictions: Surveyed recreational users will show higher intent to purchase a hearing protector that allows hearing ambient sound compared to standard models.; Sales of a specialized recreational line will exceed 5% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed effectively..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection for everyday use (e.g., sleep, home office, travel) if they perceive it as a health necessity that improves quality of life, and if the product is discreet and comfortable. Who benefits: Individuals exposed to noise in non-industrial settings who seek health protection and comfort.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it is seen as bulky, uncomfortable, or unnecessary for daily activities; a discreet, comfortable product would remove those barriers.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell higher-margin consumer earplugs through online channels and retail partnerships, leveraging existing distribution and brand reputation for safety.. Assumptions: Health awareness about noise exposure is growing among non-industrial consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay for comfort and discretion.; Existing retail channels can accommodate consumer earplugs without cannibalizing B2B sales.. Predictions: Surveyed everyday users will show higher intent to purchase a discreet hearing protector compared to standard industrial models.; Consumer earplug sales will represent at least 10% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed as a health product..

Test "Recreational vs Everyday Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified recreational users (shooting, hunting, outdoor sports) and 250 everyday users (musicians, home office, travel). Recruit via panels to match demographics.. Measure: 1) Choice: which product concept they would purchase (recreational performance model vs everyday discreet model). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP) for each concept. 3) Intent to purchase within 12 months.. Predictions: T1: Recreational users will choose the performance model at a higher rate than everyday users and will show WTP at least 20% above baseline price.; T2: Everyday users will choose the discreet model at a higher rate than recreational users and will show WTP at least 20% above baseline price.. Decision rule: If recreational users choose the performance model ≥55% and everyday users choose the discreet model ≥55%, proceed to develop differentiated propositions for each segment. If either group chooses its target model <45%, abandon that segment expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.; Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.; 2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.; 4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.; 5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business..

T1: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing consumer sales through its existing dealer network and by leveraging its engineering to produce a differentiated garden tractor.. Why behaviour changes: Rising homeownership rates in the 1950s-1960s increase the number of households with small gardens. These households seek practical, low‑maintenance solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need at an affordable price.. How value is captured: Deere can sell garden tractors through its independent dealer network, using the same engineering platform as farm tractors but scaled down. The value is captured through direct sales revenue and increased dealer traffic.. Assumptions: Homeownership trends continue to rise, providing a growing base of potential buyers.; Garden tractors remain inexpensive and practical compared to manual tools.; Deere's dealer network can effectively reach individual homeowners.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor, sales will be positively correlated with regional homeownership rates.; Consumer surveys will show that price sensitivity and ease of use are primary purchase drivers for garden tractors..

T2: Small‑farm operators will adopt a differentiated tractor proposition because they need a versatile, affordable machine that can replace multiple tools and reduce labor costs, and Deere can capture value by selling through its dealer network and offering financing. Who benefits: Deere & Company benefits by expanding its market beyond large farms to smallholders, increasing sales volume and dealer engagement.. Why behaviour changes: Post‑war agricultural mechanization and rising labor costs make small farms seek equipment that can perform multiple tasks (plowing, planting, hauling) without requiring a large crew. A tractor that is cheaper than a full‑size farm tractor. How value is captured: Deere can price a small‑farm tractor below its standard farm models, sell it through existing dealers, and offer financing to lower the entry barrier. Value is captured through higher unit volume and increased dealer traffic.. Assumptions: Small farms constitute a sizable segment with unmet equipment needs.; Labor costs are rising enough to justify mechanization.; Deere's dealer network can reach small‑farm owners.. Predictions: Sales of a differentiated small‑farm tractor will be higher in regions with a higher proportion of farms under 100 acres.; Purchasers will cite labor cost savings and task versatility as primary reasons for buying..

Test "Garden vs Small-Farm Tractor Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Stratify by homeownership status (owner vs renter) and farm ownership (own farm vs not).. Measure: 1) Choice: which tractor concept they would purchase (garden tractor vs small-farm tractor). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. 3) Primary purchase driver (price, versatility, labor cost savings, etc.).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will choose the garden tractor at a higher rate than renters, and WTP will be driven by price and ease of use.; T2: Farm owners will choose the small-farm tractor at a higher rate than non-farm owners, and WTP will be driven by labor cost savings and task versatility.. Decision rule: If homeowners choose garden tractor >55% and farm owners choose small-farm tractor >55%, proceed with differentiated proposition for the segment showing stronger preference. If either segment falls below 50% preference, abandon that segment. If both segments exceed 55%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: DIY boaters will purchase a dedicated Jotun marine coating kit if it is marketed as a premium, easy-to-apply solution that extends boat life and reduces maintenance effort. Who benefits: Jotun gains higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales and builds brand loyalty among boat owners.. Why behaviour changes: Boaters perceive professional-grade marine coatings as essential for protecting expensive assets; a simplified kit reduces perceived difficulty and time cost, making purchase worthwhile.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a branded kit, recurring repurchases for maintenance cycles, and cross-selling of complementary products through Jotun’s existing retail network.. Assumptions: Boaters value durability and are willing to pay more for proven marine-grade protection.; A simplified application process (e.g., pre-mixed, brush-on) reduces perceived effort.; Jotun’s Marine Coatings brand is trusted by boat owners for performance.. Predictions: Surveyed boaters will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a branded DIY kit than for generic marine paint.; Pilot sales through Jotun Multicolor Centers will show a conversion rate of at least 5% of foot traffic to kit purchase.; Repeat purchase rate within 12 months will exceed 30% due to maintenance needs..

T2: Homeowners will purchase a Jotun protective coating kit for decks/fences if it is marketed as a long-lasting, easy-to-apply solution that reduces maintenance frequency and protects against weathering. Who benefits: Jotun gains higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales and leverages its protective coatings expertise to enter residential markets.. Why behaviour changes: Homeowners seek durable exterior solutions to avoid frequent repainting; a branded kit that promises extended protection and simple application reduces perceived effort and cost of ownership.. How value is captured: Premium pricing for a branded kit, recurring repurchases for maintenance cycles, and cross-selling through Jotun’s existing retail network (Multicolor Centers).. Assumptions: Homeowners value durability and are willing to pay more for proven protective performance.; A simplified application process (e.g., pre-mixed, brush-on) reduces perceived effort.; Jotun’s Protective Coatings brand is trusted for weather resistance.. Test "Consumer vs Commercial Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. After exposure, ask: "How likely are you to purchase a John Deere garden tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale. Also ask: "What is the maximum price you would pay?" and "Would you recommend this to others in your segment?". The test will be run in 12 weeks with a €20,000 budget for platform fees, incentives, and data analysis.. Sample: 400 respondents (200 small‑garden households, 200 professional landscapers/small farm operators).. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each segment under each message condition.. Predictions: T1: Households with small gardens will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the consumer message than when exposed to the commercial message.; T2: Professional landscapers/small farm operators will show higher purchase intent when exposed to the commercial message than when exposed to the consumer message.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two message conditions for households with small gardens is at least 1.5 points (on the 10‑point scale) and the difference for professionals is at least 1.5 points in the opposite direction, then both theories are supported and the test is inconclusive for a single recommendation. If only one segment shows a ≥1.5‑point. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual consumers for home use (e.g., personal body‑fat monitoring).; 2) Expand the existing BIA analyser to a broader B2B market (e.g., gyms, corporate wellness programs) without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on clinic and health‑club sales.; 4) Redesign the product for a different use case (e.g., medical diagnostics, fitness‑center equipment) and pursue a new distribution channel..

T1: Individual consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, driven by awareness of body-fat links to disease. Who benefits: Consumers seeking health monitoring; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales.. Why behaviour changes: Medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes, and cancers creates perceived health risk, motivating purchase of a tool to monitor body composition.. How value is captured: Tanita can sell a differentiated consumer model at higher margins through direct-to-consumer channels, leveraging its brand reputation for medical-grade accuracy.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita's medical-grade accuracy based on professional market presence.; Health awareness campaigns in 1993 effectively communicated disease links to body fat.; Price sensitivity is secondary to health concerns for target segment.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser if presented with medical risk information.; Willingness to pay will be above €100 for a device marketed as medically accurate..

T2: Individual consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a fashion accessory or status symbol, motivated by peer influence and the desire to display health-conscious lifestyle. Who benefits: Consumers seeking social signaling; Tanita benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand extension into lifestyle markets.. Why behaviour changes: Social media and peer groups in the early 1990s increasingly valued visible health metrics as a status marker, creating demand for devices that can be displayed and shared.. How value is captured: Tanita can launch a stylized consumer model with design features, limited editions, and direct-to-consumer marketing, earning higher margins through brand premium.. Assumptions: Fashion and status motivations are significant for a segment of consumers in 1993.; Tanita's brand reputation for precision transfers to lifestyle positioning.; Price sensitivity is lower for status-driven purchases.. Predictions: Consumers will express intent to purchase a home body-fat analyser when presented with fashion/status framing.; Willingness to pay will be above €150 for a device marketed as a lifestyle accessory..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical vs Fashion Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 adult consumers in Japan (target demographic: 25-55 years, health/fitness interest). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Medical framing (emphasize disease risk and medical-grade accuracy) or Fashion framing (emphasize lifestyle status and design). After viewing the message, ask: 1) "Would you purchase a home body-fat analyser?" (yes/no). 2) "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open numeric). 3) "How important is medical accuracy vs. style?" (1-5 scale).. Sample: 400 consumers, balanced across message conditions (200 each).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Medical framing will yield higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than fashion framing.; T2: Fashion framing will yield higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than medical framing.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for medical framing exceeds fashion framing by at least 15 percentage points (e.g., 55% vs 40%), proceed with medical-focused consumer proposition. If fashion framing exceeds medical framing by at least 15 percentage points, pursue fashion/lifestyle positioning. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Propose a low-cost consumer messaging test (X1) to validate demand before committing to product development. Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet, as public evidence from 1993 does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay or demand for home body-fat analysers. The evidence base is insufficient to justify the investment without empirical validation of consumer intent. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T1 revised: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) is explicitly marked as synthetic and unrelated to consumer demand, so it does not support or contradict T1. However, the lack of any real evidence supporting T1 (consumer demand for home use) means the theory remains unproven. The revised claim should reflect that T1 is still a hypothesis requiring validation, not a fact. New claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, driven by awareness of body-fat links to disease. This claim remains a hypothesis requiring empirical validation of consumer intent and willingness to pay.. Evidence: tanita-dic-origin.

This would not directly support or contradict T1 (medical necessity driving adoption), but it would reinforce that operational efficiency alone does not create consumer demand. This claim remains a hypothesis requiring empirical validation of consumer intent and willingness to pay. Operational improvements alone do not create demand.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence from 1993 does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for individual buyers. T1: DIY boat owners will purchase Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the product as a premium, professional-grade solution that saves time and ensures durability, because they value reliability and are willing to pay more for a trusted brand. Who benefits: Jotun benefits by capturing higher-margin consumer sales and building brand loyalty among boat owners.. Why behaviour changes: Boat owners currently rely on specialized marine suppliers or generic paints; a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes professional-grade performance and ease of use would shift their purchasing behavior toward Jotun.. How value is captured: Jotun would sell directly to consumers through its Multicolor Centers and online channels at premium prices, retaining full margin and brand control.. Assumptions: DIY boat owners have sufficient budget for premium coatings.; They trust brand reputation as a proxy for performance.; Jotun can effectively communicate professional-grade benefits to consumers.. Predictions: Surveyed DIY boat owners will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a Jotun-branded marine coating compared to generic alternatives.; Sales of Jotun marine coatings through consumer channels will grow faster than overall marine segment growth if a differentiated proposition is launched..

T2: DIY boat owners will purchase Jotun marine coatings if they receive clear, easy-to-follow application instructions and a user-friendly product format (e.g., pre-mixed, ready-to-apply), because they lack technical expertise and want a hassle-free experience. Who benefits: Jotun benefits by expanding its consumer market share and increasing volume sales through lower-friction purchases.. Why behaviour changes: Current DIY boat owners avoid professional-grade coatings due to perceived complexity; simplifying the application process would reduce perceived risk and encourage trial.. How value is captured: Jotun would capture value through higher volume sales and potentially lower margins, but increased market penetration and brand awareness could lead to cross-selling of other products.. Assumptions: DIY boat owners prioritize ease of use over premium performance.; They are willing to pay a modest premium for convenience.; Jotun can develop and communicate simplified application instructions effectively.. Predictions: DIY boat owners will report higher intent to purchase when presented with a product featuring step-by-step instructions and pre-mixed formulation compared to a standard professional-grade product.; Sales of Jotun marine coatings in consumer channels will increase when a simplified product is introduced, even if price remains similar to generic alternatives..

Test "DIY Boat Owner Preference Test: Premium Brand vs Simplified Application" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 400 DIY boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media, balanced across age and boat ownership experience.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay premium (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more for Jotun-branded product). 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy vs would not). 3) Preference for simplified application (percentage choosing product with step-by-step instructions and pre-mixed format).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of respondents will indicate willingness to pay a 20% premium for a Jotun-branded marine coating, and purchase intent will be higher for the premium-branded option than for a generic alternative.; T2: At least 60% of respondents will choose the simplified-application version (step-by-step instructions, pre-mixed) over the standard professional-grade version, even if price is identical, and purchase intent will be higher for the simplified version.. Decision rule: If the premium-branded option achieves ≥60% willingness to pay and purchase intent ≥55%, proceed with premium consumer proposition (supports T1). If the simplified-application option achieves ≥60% preference and purchase intent ≥55%, proceed with simplified consumer proposition (supports T2). If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Propose a consumer proposition for DIY boat owners emphasizing professional-grade performance and brand trust (T1), but only after running the proposed test X1 to validate willingness to pay premium. Current evidence is insufficient to justify investment without testing. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 revised: The simulated result SYN-D is explicitly marked as synthetic and not real data, so it cannot be used to support or contradict T1. However, if we hypothetically treated it as real evidence of operational efficiency in packaging, it would suggest Jotun has the manufacturing capability to produce consumer-friendly formats, which is a prerequisite for T2 (simplified application). Since SYN-D is not real, no revision is w New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Current public evidence does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or Jotun's reach to individual buyers for marine coatings. The evidence base is neutral across all theories. A test is required before committing capital. Target customer: DIY boat owners (leisure yacht owners performing maintenance). Value proposition: Professional-grade marine coating performance with consumer-friendly application (T1) OR simplified application format (T2). Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed test X1 (DIY Boat Owner Preference Test) to validate willingness to pay premium vs. preference for simplified application before making an investment decision.. Uncertainty: High. No public evidence confirms consumer demand for Jotun marine coatings, willingness to pay a premium, or Jotun's existing consumer distribution reach. All evidence is neutral or company claims without consumer validation.. Would change if: Evidence shows Jotun already sells marine coatings to consumers through Multicolor Centers at scale.; Independent study confirms DIY boat owners prefer Jotun brand over generic alternatives.; Market data shows declining generic marine coating sales and rising demand for premium DIY options.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Homeownership of one-family detached homes rose significantly in the 1950s, modestly in the 1960s and 1970s, dropped slightly in the 1980s, and shows an extremely small increased in the 1990s, reaching 87 percent in 2000 (see graph).

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Because of this, many John Deere dealers were selling some of these lines or other brands of lawn and garden tractors because Deere didn’t offer any.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.; Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.. T1: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.. Why behaviour changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, practical solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.. How value is captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and its engineering expertise to differentiate from competitors.. Assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.; Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.; Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales of lawn and garden tractors will increase relative to competitors.; Surveyed small garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for Deere's engineering and brand.; Deere's dealer network will report higher foot traffic and accessory sales from garden tractor buyers..

T2: Professional landscapers and small farm operators will adopt garden tractors because they need reliable, efficient equipment for commercial work, and they value Deere's engineering reputation for durability and service support. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by selling higher-margin commercial-grade tractors and attachments through its dealer network, leveraging its established service infrastructure.. Why behaviour changes: Commercial users require equipment that can handle continuous use and offers quick parts/service availability; Deere's reputation for robust engineering and dealer support makes it attractive.. How value is captured: Deere can price commercial tractors at a premium, sell service contracts, and increase attachment sales, capturing value through both equipment and ongoing service revenue.. Assumptions: Commercial landscaping and small farm markets are growing in the 1960s.; Deere's dealer network provides adequate service coverage for commercial users.; Commercial buyers prioritize reliability and service over price.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated commercial garden tractor proposition, sales to professional landscapers will increase relative to competitors.; Commercial buyers will report higher satisfaction with Deere's service support compared to other brands.; Deere's dealer network will see increased service contract uptake from commercial customers..

Decision rule: If recreational users choose the performance model ≥55% and everyday users choose the discreet model ≥55%, proceed to develop differentiated propositions for each segment. If either group chooses its target model <45%, abandon that segment expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Who benefits: Recreational users who need situational awareness and comfort while engaging in noisy activities.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it mutes sound and reduces enjoyment; a product that preserves audio clarity and comfort would remove that barrier.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for specialized features (e.g., active listening, FM radio) and sell directly to consumers through e-commerce, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Recreational market size is sufficient to justify dedicated product line.; Consumers are willing to pay for performance-enhancing features.; Brand perception of safety does not deter recreational buyers.. Predictions: Surveyed recreational users will show higher intent to purchase a hearing protector that allows hearing ambient sound compared to standard models.; Sales of a specialized recreational line will exceed 5% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed effectively..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection for everyday use (e.g., sleep, home office, travel) if they perceive it as a health necessity that improves quality of life, and if the product is discreet and comfortable. Who benefits: Individuals exposed to noise in non-industrial settings who seek health protection and comfort.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it is seen as bulky, uncomfortable, or unnecessary for daily activities; a discreet, comfortable product would remove those barriers.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell higher-margin consumer earplugs through online channels and retail partnerships, leveraging existing distribution and brand reputation for safety.. Assumptions: Health awareness about noise exposure is growing among non-industrial consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay for comfort and discretion.; Existing retail channels can accommodate consumer earplugs without cannibalizing B2B sales.. Predictions: Surveyed everyday users will show higher intent to purchase a discreet hearing protector compared to standard industrial models.; Consumer earplug sales will represent at least 10% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed as a health product..

If either group chooses its target model <45%, abandon that segment expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Because of this, many John Deere dealers were selling some of these lines or other brands of lawn and garden tractors because Deere didn’t offer any.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

T1: Homeowners with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.. Why behaviour changes: Rising homeownership rates in the 1950s-60s increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek practical, low‑maintenance solutions for yard work, and garden tractors meet that need.. How value is captured: Deere can sell garden tractors at premium prices through its dealer network, using its brand reputation and engineering to differentiate from competitors.. Assumptions: Homeownership trends continue to rise in the 1960s.; Small‑garden households are willing to pay a premium for a branded, reliable garden tractor.; Deere's dealer network can effectively reach these households.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor, sales will be positively correlated with regional homeownership rates.; Surveyed homeowners will rank garden tractors as a preferred tool for yard work compared to manual tools..

T2: Small‑farm operators will adopt garden tractors because they need a versatile, low‑cost machine for multiple chores, and Deere’s existing dealer network can reach them, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by selling garden tractors to small‑farm operators through its dealer network, leveraging its engineering to offer a differentiated product.. Why behaviour changes: Small‑farm operators face labor constraints and need a single machine that can handle plowing, mowing, and other tasks; a garden tractor provides that versatility at a lower cost than larger farm equipment.. How value is captured: Deere can price garden tractors competitively while maintaining margins through its dealer network, using its brand reputation to differentiate from generic competitors.. Assumptions: Small‑farm operators are a significant segment of Deere’s potential market in the 1960s.; They are willing to purchase through existing dealers rather than direct sales.; Deere’s engineering can be adapted to meet their specific needs without major redesign.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor, sales will be positively correlated with the density of small‑farm operations in a region.; Small‑farm operators will rank garden tractors as a preferred tool for multiple chores compared to separate machines..

Test "Regional Purchase Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Survey homeowners and small-farm operators in two regions with different demographic profiles: Region A (high homeownership, low small-farm density) and Region B (low homeownership, high small-farm density). Offer a choice between a branded Deere garden tractor (differentiated proposition) and a generic competitor model at the same price. Track actual purchase decisions or stated intent to purchase.. Sample: 200 respondents per region (100 homeowners, 100 small-farm operators), recruited via local agricultural extension offices and homeowner associations.. Measure: Percentage of respondents who choose the Deere branded tractor over the generic model.. Predictions: T1: In Region A, homeowners will choose the Deere branded tractor at a rate at least 10 percentage points higher than in Region B, because homeownership drives demand for garden tractors.; T2: In Region B, small-farm operators will choose the Deere branded tractor at a rate at least 10 percentage points higher than in Region A, because small-farm needs drive demand for versatile garden tractors.. Decision rule: If the difference in Deere choice rate between Region A and Region B is ≥10 percentage points and aligns with T1 (higher in Region A), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If the difference aligns with T2 (higher in Region B), target small-farm operators. If the difference is <10 percentage points, no. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

The evidence of rising homeownership and independent observations of demand for garden tractors supports T1, while T2 lacks direct evidence of small-farm operator demand for garden tractors specifically. Target customer: Homeowners with small gardens. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical vs Fashion Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 adult consumers in Japan (target demographic: 25-55 years, health/fitness interest). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: Medical framing (emphasize disease risk and medical-grade accuracy) or Fashion framing (emphasize lifestyle status and design). After viewing the message, ask: 1) "Would you purchase a home body-fat analyser?" (yes/no). 2) "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open numeric). 3) "How important is medical accuracy vs. style?" (1-5 scale).. Sample: 400 consumers, balanced across message conditions (200 each).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Medical framing will yield higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than fashion framing.; T2: Fashion framing will yield higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than medical framing.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for medical framing exceeds fashion framing by at least 15 percentage points (e.g., 55% vs 40%), proceed with medical-focused consumer proposition. If fashion framing exceeds medical framing by at least 15 percentage points, pursue fashion/lifestyle positioning. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt hearing protection for recreational activities (e.g., shooting, hunting, outdoor sports) if they perceive it as enhancing performance and safety without compromising enjoyment. Who benefits: Recreational users who need situational awareness and comfort while engaging in noisy activities.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it mutes sound and reduces enjoyment; a product that preserves audio clarity and comfort would remove that barrier.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge premium prices for specialized features (e.g., active listening, FM radio) and sell directly to consumers through e-commerce, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Recreational market size is sufficient to justify dedicated product line.; Consumers are willing to pay for performance-enhancing features.; Brand perception of safety does not deter recreational buyers.. Predictions: Surveyed recreational users will show higher intent to purchase a hearing protector that allows hearing ambient sound compared to standard models.; Sales of a specialized recreational line will exceed 5% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed effectively..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection for everyday use (e.g., sleep, home office, travel) if they perceive it as a health necessity that improves quality of life, and if the product is discreet and comfortable. Who benefits: Individuals exposed to noise in non-industrial settings who seek health protection and comfort.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid hearing protection because it is seen as bulky, uncomfortable, or unnecessary for daily activities; a discreet, comfortable product would remove those barriers.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell higher-margin consumer earplugs through online channels and retail partnerships, leveraging existing distribution and brand reputation for safety.. Assumptions: Health awareness about noise exposure is growing among non-industrial consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay for comfort and discretion.; Existing retail channels can accommodate consumer earplugs without cannibalizing B2B sales.. Predictions: Surveyed everyday users will show higher intent to purchase a discreet hearing protector compared to standard industrial models.; Consumer earplug sales will represent at least 10% of total revenue within 12 months if marketed as a health product..

Test "Recreational vs Everyday Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay questions.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 recruited via shooting/hunting/outdoor sports forums (recreational segment) and 250 via general consumer panels (everyday segment).. Measure: 1) Choice: which product concept they would purchase (recreational performance model vs everyday discreet model). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP) for each concept. 3) Intent to recommend.. Predictions: T1: Recreational participants will choose the performance model at a higher rate than everyday participants and will show higher WTP for it.; T2: Everyday participants will choose the discreet model at a higher rate than recreational participants and will show higher WTP for it.. Decision rule: If recreational participants choose the performance model in ≥60% of choices AND their average WTP for it is at least 20% higher than for the everyday model, then T1 is supported. If everyday participants choose the discreet model in ≥60% of choices AND their average WTP for it is at least 20% higher than for the performance model, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Propose a low-cost test to validate consumer demand before committing to a differentiated proposition. Given the lack of direct evidence for either theory, T1 is slightly more favoured due to existing competitor activity (Sordin X2) and Hellberg's existing electronic product line, but both remain unproven. Recommend declining the full test budget in favor of a smaller, targeted experiment or further evidence search. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence base is insufficient to validate either the recreational (T1) or everyday (T2) use case. While T1 has some indirect support from competitor activity (Sordin X2) and Hellberg's existing electronic product line, there is no direct evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or market size for either segment. The proposed test (X1) is the most Target customer: Recreational shooting/hunting/outdoor sports enthusiasts (for T1) or everyday noise-exposed individuals (for T2). Value proposition: T1: Performance-enhancing hearing protection that preserves situational awareness and comfort for recreational activities. T2: Discreet, comfortable hearing protection for everyday health protection.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct a low-cost, targeted experiment (e.g., online survey with 200-300 participants) to validate consumer demand and willingness to pay before investing in product development and marketing. Alternatively, explore partnership/licensing (. Uncertainty: High uncertainty regarding consumer demand, willingness to pay, and market size for both recreational and everyday hearing protection use cases. Competitor activity (Sordin X2) suggests potential demand, but Hellberg's ability to capture it. Would change if: Evidence of strong consumer demand for recreational hearing protection (e.g., high search volume, existing market size data).; Evidence of Hellberg's existing consumer distribution channels or brand recognition among individual buyers.; Competitor failure to gain traction in the recreational hearing protection market.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Assumptions: Recreational boaters are aware of PLB regulations and seek compliant safety gear.; There is sufficient demand for a differentiated product beyond existing generic PLBs.; ACR can design a product that meets boater preferences (e.g., size, durability).. How value is captured: ACR can sell through insurance brokers or directly to insurers, capturing volume sales and possibly bundling with other marine safety products.. Assumptions: Insurance regulators or insurers view PLBs as risk mitigation tools.; There is a market of insurers willing to offer subsidies or require PLBs for policyholders.; ACR can meet any insurance-specific requirements (e.g., durability, data reporting).. Predictions: If offered, at least 15% of surveyed boaters with insurance would indicate they would purchase a PLB if their insurer required or subsidized it.; Sales would be higher in regions with higher marine insurance penetration..

Test "Boater Preference Survey with Insurance Incentive" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey of recreational boaters in coastal states, presenting two product concepts: (1) a differentiated PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700; (2) the same PLB offered with a $200 insurance subsidy (effective price $500) and a statement that insurers may require it. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay. The survey also asks about current safety gear ownership and insurance status.. Sample: 500 recreational boaters recruited via boating clubs and marine forums, stratified by state (California, Florida, Washington) to reflect high boater participation. Recruitment cost estimated €2,000.. Measure: Purchase intent rate for the differentiated product (T1) vs. purchase intent rate when insurance subsidy is offered (T2). Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the differentiated product.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent will be at least 10% for the differentiated product at $700, and will not increase significantly when a subsidy is offered (difference <5 percentage points).; T2: Purchase intent will increase by at least 10 percentage points when the insurance subsidy is offered, indicating that price reduction and insurer involvement drive adoption.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent for the differentiated product at $700 is ≥10% AND the increase in intent when subsidy is offered is <5 percentage points, then T1 is supported and ACR should pursue a differentiated consumer proposition. If the increase is ≥10 percentage points, T2 is supported and ACR should explore insurance partnership. If neither condition is met, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Boater Willingness-to-Pay Survey with Insurance Subsidy Scenario" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey of recreational boaters in the United States, recruited via boating forums and marine insurance provider lists. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Standard PLB description with suggested retail price $700; (2) Same description plus a statement that marine insurance companies offer a $200 discount for PLB ownership (effectively $500). Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay (WTP) and whether they would purchase. The survey also asks about insurance status (insured vs uninsured).. Sample: 400 boaters (200 per condition), balanced for region and experience level.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars and purchase intent (binary).. Predictions: T1: WTP will be high (≥$500) regardless of subsidy, because boaters value safety and are willing to pay premium; purchase intent will be similar across conditions.; T2: WTP will be significantly higher in the subsidy condition (≈$500) than in the standard condition (≈$300), because the discount makes the device affordable; purchase intent will be higher among insured boaters in the subsidy condition.. Decision rule: If average WTP in the subsidy condition is at least $450 and purchase intent among insured boaters in that condition exceeds 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition with insurance partnerships. If WTP in the standard condition is below $400, reject the premium pricing approach. If neither condition meets thresholds, decline expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Propose test X1 to validate willingness-to-pay and insurance subsidy impact before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. Do not invest in product development yet. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

The company should continue focusing on existing B2B markets Target customer: Commercial marine, military, and aircraft operators (existing markets). Value proposition: Reliable 406 MHz distress beacon for professional and commercial use. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Conduct a small-scale willingness-to-pay survey (as proposed in test X1) before committing to product development. Uncertainty: High uncertainty about consumer demand and price sensitivity. No evidence of insurance involvement. Regulatory approval does not equal market adoption.. Would change if: Evidence of insurance mandates or subsidies for PLBs; Market research showing high purchase intent among recreational boaters at $700; Competitor announcements of consumer-focused PLBs with strong sales. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Sample: 200 individual creators recruited via creator forums and social media (100 per product concept), balanced for experience level (novice vs. established).. Measure: Conversion rate (purchase vs. non-purchase), average order value (EUR), and satisfaction score (1-10).. Predictions: T1: Premium-branded single mic will achieve higher conversion and higher average order value than the integrated kit, because creators value status and professional image.; T2: Integrated kit will achieve higher conversion and higher average order value than the premium single mic, because creators prioritize ease of use and integrated workflow.. Decision rule: If premium-branded mic conversion rate >= 12% and its average order value is at least 20% higher than the kit, proceed with differentiated premium line (supports T1). T1: DIY boat owners will adopt a differentiated consumer marine coating product if it is positioned as a premium, easy‑to‑apply solution that saves time and reduces professional service costs. Who benefits: Jotun would capture higher margins through premium pricing and direct‑to‑consumer sales; DIY boat owners benefit from lower total cost of ownership and convenience.. Why behaviour changes: DIY boat owners currently rely on professional services for maintenance, which is costly and time‑consuming. A product that simplifies application and offers superior protection would shift their purchasing behavior from service contracts. How value is captured: Jotun would sell the product through its existing Multicolor Centers and online channels, retaining brand control and earning premium prices compared to standard marine coatings.. Assumptions: DIY boat owners represent a sizable, reachable segment within Jotun’s existing retail network.; They are willing to pay a premium for convenience and performance.; Jotun can adapt its marine coating formulation for consumer use without compromising performance.. Predictions: If offered, at least 15% of surveyed DIY boat owners would indicate intent to purchase within 12 months.; Average willingness to pay would be at least 20% above current professional coating prices..

T2: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated consumer protective coating product for decks/fences if it is marketed as a long‑lasting, low‑maintenance solution that reduces repainting frequency and effort. Who benefits: Jotun would capture higher margins through premium pricing and direct‑to‑consumer sales; homeowners benefit from reduced maintenance costs and time savings.. Why behaviour changes: Homeowners currently repaint decks/fences every 3‑5 years due to wear and weathering. A coating that extends service life and simplifies application would shift their purchasing behavior from periodic repainting to a single, longer‑lasting. How value is captured: Jotun would sell the product through its Multicolor Centers and online channels, leveraging existing retail reach to reach homeowners directly and earn premium prices compared to standard protective coatings.. Assumptions: Homeowners represent a sizable, reachable segment within Jotun’s existing retail network.; They are willing to pay a premium for reduced maintenance frequency and effort.; Jotun can adapt its protective coating formulation for consumer use without compromising performance.. Predictions: If offered, at least 15% of surveyed homeowners would indicate intent to purchase within 12 months.; Average willingness to pay would be at least 20% above current protective coating prices..

Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified recreational users (shooting, hunting, outdoor sports) and 250 everyday users (musicians, home office, travel). Recruit via panels to match demographics..
